lessons.title: How memory works
lessons.anchor: Use a familiar image or meaningful connection to recover something new.
lessons.outcome: Try recall before reveal, compare with the model, and return after another task.
lessons.sources: Original presentation slides 7–10; current A2 row 4. Earlier first20 memory draft used as an adaptation reference.
lessons.decisions: The current plan uses familiar pictures and delayed recall. The old timed number/date demonstration is not inserted into this route; no learning-speed claim is carried over.

screens.title: Try before looking
screens.text:
Welcome to Hebleo. Throughout this course, we will connect new Hebrew to something you already know. Before we meet any letters, try a small memory experiment.
You will see three familiar objects. Look at them, then hide them and try to name them. This is practice, not a score of your memory.

screens.title: Look, hide, remember
screens.text: Press Show pictures. Name each object in a language you know. When you are ready, press Hide pictures and tell yourself what was there.
assets: IMAGE MEMORY-OBJECTS: three separate, equally clear pictures: a plain drinking cup, a door key, and an apple. No printed labels while visible. Provide equivalent spoken descriptions for nonvisual use.
CONTROL: Show pictures → Hide pictures → spoken or typed attempt → Reveal pictures. No timer. Reveal is also available after “I cannot recall yet”.

interaction.prompt: After hiding the pictures, name the three objects.
interaction.feedback: Compare object identities, in any order. Synonyms and any language are fine. Missing an object is a reason to look again, not a failure.

screens.title: Make a connection
screens.text:
Now give the objects a familiar setting. Imagine an apple beside your usual cup, with your key between them. If that setting is unfamiliar, choose one of your own.
The useful part is the connection you can bring back to mind. It does not have to be clever or the same as someone else’s. When we learn letters, a familiar image can help you recover a shape and its sound.

screens.title: Do something else briefly
screens.text: Leave the three objects for a moment. Look at the shapes below and choose the one that matches the outline. Then continue without reopening the pictures.
assets: IMAGE MEMORY-SHAPES: unlabelled triangle outline; response shapes circle, triangle, square. Accessible labels identify the three shapes. For nonvisual use, prompt “Which of these shapes has three sides?”

interaction.prompt: Which shape matches the triangular outline?

feedback.circle: A circle has a curved edge. Look for three sides.
feedback.triangle: Yes. The outline has three sides.
feedback.square: A square has four sides. Look for three.

screens.title: Try again after a gap
screens.text:
Before looking back, name the objects once more. If it helps, revisit the scene you imagined. Then compare with the pictures.
We will use this rhythm in the course: meet something new, connect it to something familiar, try to recall it, and meet it again later.

interaction.prompt: Name the three objects again before revealing them.
interaction.feedback: Compare with the same three pictures. Notice which connection helped you; neither improvement nor perfect recall is required.

check.answer: It connects the new item to something familiar to you.
options: It connects the new item to something familiar to you.
It guarantees that you will never forget.

feedback.It connects the new item to something fa: Yes. A familiar connection gives you a way back to the new item.
A simple connection can work. Complexity is not the aim.
feedback.It guarantees that you will never forget: You may still forget. Recall and later practice remain part of learning.

apply.prompt: Choose one of the three objects. Describe a familiar place, experience or image that helps you remember it.
apply.answer: Any connection the learner can explain, such as “the cup I use at breakfast”.
apply.feedback: Self-check: is the connection familiar, and does it lead back to the chosen object? There is no single correct scene.

lessons.ending: You have tried connecting, recalling and returning after a gap. Next, we will use those moves to learn four Hebrew letter shapes.

lessons.title: Letters 1: מנתל — four consonants
lessons.anchor: Recover the shape through a familiar image, then retrieve the sound without the image.
lessons.outcome: Recognise and type מ, נ, ת and ל from their sounds.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 6 and 10; Hebleo Mnemonics slides 2 and 6; current A2 row 5. Earlier first20 MNT prose adapted, with ל added and final forms removed.
lessons.decisions: Preserve Guy’s mountain-climber, nose, tripping and ladle anchors. The actual drawings remain original-asset placeholders. No final-form teaching in this lesson.

screens.title: Two shapes, two sounds
screens.text:
מ represents /m/, the sound at the start of mountain. Its name is Mem.
נ represents /n/, the sound at the start of nose. Its name is Nun.
Listen to each sound and look at its letter. Focus on connecting the sound to the printed shape; you do not need to memorise the letter names yet.
assets: AUDIO MNTL-M: isolated /m/; AUDIO MNTL-N: isolated /n/. Play on request, without adding a vowel.
IMAGE MNTL-M and MNTL-N: Guy’s original mountain-climber and nose mnemonic drawings, paired with the exact block letters.

screens.title: Recover the first pair
screens.text: Hide the pictures. Try to recognise the letters from their sounds. If you need help, bring the familiar image back to mind.

feedback.מ: מ represents /m/. The sound you heard was /n/.
feedback.נ: Yes: נ represents /n/, as in nose.

screens.title: Two more shapes
screens.text:
ת represents /t/, as at the start of tripping. Its name is Tav.
ל represents /l/, as at the start of ladle. Its name is Lamed.
Use the tripping image for ת and the ladle image for ל. Say each sound, look away, and picture the printed shape.
assets: AUDIO MNTL-T: isolated /t/; AUDIO MNTL-L: isolated /l/.
IMAGE MNTL-T and MNTL-L: Guy’s original tripping and ladle drawings. Preserve the source drawing rather than substituting a new mnemonic.

screens.title: Make the shape yourself
screens.text:
Choose the matching printed letter on the Hebrew keyboard. You may use the on-screen keyboard.
Copying a visible shape helps you locate its key. In the next exercise, the shape will be hidden so that you can try to recall it.
assets: KEYBOARD: highlight the matching key only during copying. Hide the highlight for recall questions.

interaction.feedback: Correct: ל. Use the same printed form; handwriting is not required.

feedback.נ: נ is /n/. Think of tripping for /t/.
feedback.מ: מ is /m/. Think of tripping for /t/.
feedback.ל: ל is /l/. Think of tripping for /t/.

apply.prompt: Match each sound to its printed letter.
apply.feedback: מ = /m/, נ = /n/, ת = /t/, ל = /l/. Replay a missed sound, then retry it without the mnemonic.
apply.stimulus: Left-hand prompts: /m/; /n/; /t/; /l/

apply.prompt: Listen and type the printed letter.
apply.feedback: The matching letter is מ; its sound is /m/.
apply.stimulus: AUDIO MNTL-MEM: isolated /m/.

apply.prompt: Listen and type the printed letter.
apply.feedback: The matching letter is ל; its sound is /l/.
apply.stimulus: AUDIO MNTL-LAMED: isolated /l/.

apply.prompt: Read the sounds of these letters aloud: ל  מ  ת  נ.
apply.feedback: Reveal the four individual sound buttons and compare one at a time. This is self-check, not automatic pronunciation scoring.

lessons.ending: You can now connect four printed letters to their sounds. Next, you will see how Hebrew arranges them and what happens to מ and נ at the end of a word.

lessons.title: Writing 1: right-to-left and final forms ם/ן
lessons.anchor: Keep the sound from the previous lesson while changing position or final shape.
lessons.outcome: Follow Hebrew from right to left and choose מ/ם and נ/ן by word position.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 11–14; current A2 row 6. Earlier first20 writing explanation adapted.
lessons.decisions: Letter strings below are position practice, not vocabulary or full decoding. Block-letter typing is required; handwriting is optional outside the core lesson.

screens.title: Find the beginning
screens.text:
Hebrew words run from right to left. Start with the letter on the right.
מנתל
In this practice string, the order is מ, then נ, then ת, then ל. Name the letter sounds separately. We have not yet added the vowel sounds needed to read a whole word.
assets: HIGHLIGHT WRITING-DIRECTION: mark the rightmost מ first, then נ, ת and ל. Step through on taps; retain an arrow pointing left. Treat מנתל as a practice string with no assigned meaning.

screens.title: One sound, two shapes
screens.text:
מ has a different shape when it is the last letter of a word: ם. Both forms represent /m/.
מ → ם
In the middle or at the beginning, use מ. At the end, use ם. Since Hebrew runs right to left, the end of a word is on its left.
assets: POSITION DIAGRAM: show מ in the first slot of a three-slot RTL word, then ם in the final slot. The slots are boxes, not additional letters.

screens.title: The same idea with נ
screens.text:
נ also has a final shape: ן. Both forms represent /n/.
נ → ן
ת and ל keep their ordinary shapes at the end. A final form changes the letter’s shape, not its sound.

interaction.prompt: Which shape represents /n/ at the end of a word?

feedback.נ: Use נ before the end; at the end use ן.
feedback.ן: Yes. ן is final Nun, still /n/.
feedback.ם: ם is final Mem, with the sound /m/.

screens.title: Print and handwriting
screens.text:
These are printed, or block, letters. They are the forms you will read and type here. Hebrew also has handwritten forms, often called script.
You can learn handwriting with the optional practice sheet. You do not need to trace letters or learn script to complete this lesson.
assets: OPTIONAL DOWNLOAD WRITING-SCRIPT: Guy’s handwriting sheet for the taught letters only; link pending. Do not display a broken download button before the asset is supplied.

check.prompt: Which letter comes first when you follow מנתל in Hebrew reading order?

feedback.ל: ל is on the left, at the end of this string.
feedback.נ: נ comes after מ. Start at the right.
feedback.מ: Yes. Start at the rightmost מ.

apply.prompt: Match the ordinary shape to its end-of-word shape.
apply.feedback: Only מ and נ change shape among the four letters taught so far.
apply.stimulus: Left-hand prompts: מ; נ; ת; ל

apply.prompt: Type the end-of-word form of מ.
apply.feedback: Use ם at the end; it still represents /m/.

apply.prompt: Type the end-of-word form of נ.
apply.feedback: Use ן at the end; it still represents /n/.

apply.prompt: What changes when מ becomes ם?
apply.answer: The shape changes because of its position.
options: The shape changes because of its position.

feedback.The shape changes because of its positio: Yes. ם is the end-of-word form.
Both forms follow the same right-to-left reading direction.

lessons.ending: Read Hebrew from the right. At the end of a word, מ becomes ם and נ becomes ן. Next, small marks will help you add vowel sounds to the letters you know.

lessons.title: Vowels 1: a/e/i
lessons.anchor: Keep the same known consonant and change only its vowel mark.
lessons.outcome: Read the supplied a/e/i syllables and distinguish the demonstrated vowel signs.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 18–30; mnemonics a / elephant eyes / itsy-bitsy dot; current A2 row 7. Earlier first20 vowel explanation narrowed to a/e/i.
lessons.decisions: No o/u or general sheva lesson here. Alternative a/e signs are compared only in these supplied readings; source claims that all similar signs are interchangeable are not carried forward.

screens.title: Give a familiar letter a vowel
screens.text:
You know מ as /m/. Add a vowel and you can say a syllable.
מַ — /ma/
מֶ — /me/
מִ — /mi/
The letter stays the same. The marks below it change the vowel. These dots and lines are called Nikkud. Listen to the three models before trying them yourself.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS-MA, VOWELS-ME, VOWELS-MI: /ma/, /me/, /mi/, one separate recording each. The English sound labels are approximations; the native model is the target.

screens.title: The a sound
screens.text:
Look at the horizontal line in מַ. It supplies /a/: /ma/. Guy’s reminder is an open “aaaa” sound.
In these examples, מַ and מָ are both read /ma/. Their signs look different, but the supplied readings are the same. Learn to recognise both; you do not have to choose which sign to write.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS-A-PAIR: מַ, מָ, each /ma/. Display both pointed forms.

screens.title: The e sound
screens.text:
מֶ and מֵ are both read /me/ in these examples. Both signs contain a horizontal pair of dots. Guy’s image is a pair of elephant eyes.
These are reading supports for the examples in front of you. They are not a rule that you may swap vowel signs freely.

feedback.מַ: מַ is /ma/. Look for the e dots.
feedback.מִ: מִ is /mi/. It has a single dot below the letter.

screens.title: One small dot for i
screens.text:
מִ has one dot below the letter and is read /mi/. Think of one itsy-bitsy dot.
Now transfer the same signs to another familiar consonant:
נַ — /na/
נֶ — /ne/
נִ — /ni/
First recover the consonant, then add the vowel.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS-N-SET: separate /na/, /ne/, /ni/ recordings.

screens.title: Read a short practice string
screens.text:
Read from right to left, one letter-and-vowel unit at a time.
מַנִלָ
Here the practice reading is /ma-ni-la/. This is a decoding string, not a vocabulary item. Its job is to let you combine familiar letters and vowel signs.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS-STRING: /ma-ni-la/. Reveal only after the learner’s first spoken attempt.

check.prompt: Listen and choose the matching syllable.

apply.prompt: Match each written syllable to its sound.
apply.feedback: Read the consonant first, then the supplied vowel. The two-dot sign in מֵ is /e/ in this example.
apply.stimulus: Left-hand prompts: תַ; לֶ; נִ; מֵ

apply.prompt: Write the reading of מַ in English letters.
apply.feedback: מ gives /m/ and the line supplies /a/: ma.

apply.prompt: Write the practice reading of מַנִלָ in English letters.
apply.feedback: Start on the right: ma, ni, la. This is a practice string, not a new word.

apply.prompt: Read aloud: תִ · נָ · לֵ · מֶ.
apply.feedback: Reveal the four native recordings after your attempt and compare one unit at a time.
apply.stimulus: AUDIO VOWELS-READBACK: separate /ti/, /na/, /le/, /me/ recordings.

lessons.ending: You can combine familiar consonants with a, e and i. Next, three more letters will let you read your first set of useful words.

lessons.title: Letters 2: אהי
lessons.anchor: Use known vowel sounds and consonants to decode meaningful words.
lessons.outcome: Recognise א/ה/י in supplied words and retrieve six meanings: אמא, ים, מים, מתנה, יין and מנה.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 33–39; Hebleo Mnemonics אהי page; Masterfile rows 2–4, 7–8 and 10; current A2 row 8.
lessons.decisions: Word-specific readings precede general spelling rules. ים/מים are deliberately contrasted after each has its own meaning cue. The nouns are practised with clear contexts and images; sentence grammar has not yet been taught.

screens.title: Meet א
screens.text:
א is called Alef. It is not an English a. In the words you meet here, listen for the vowel carried by the letter and for any separation between sounds.
אִמָא — mother
Listen, then read the word. The beginning is /i/, followed by /ma/. The last א does not add another sound in this model. Learn this word from its whole spoken form.
assets: IMAGE AHY-ALEF: Guy’s original albatross/eagle mnemonic paired with א.
AUDIO AHY-IMA: אמא, mother. IMAGE AHY-MOTHER: a clearly captioned English scenario “a child’s mother”; do not expect appearance alone to establish the relationship.

screens.title: Meet ה
screens.text:
ה is called Heh. It can represent /h/, a breathy sound from the throat. Guy’s shape reminder is a throat.
מַתָּנָה — gift
In this word’s ending, the ה does not add /h/: listen to /ma-ta-na/. Follow the supplied word model; this is not a rule that every ה is silent.
assets: IMAGE AHY-HEH: original throat mnemonic. AUDIO AHY-H: isolated /h/. AUDIO AHY-MATANA: מתנה.
IMAGE AHY-GIFT: wrapped present being offered; alt description “a gift”.

screens.title: Meet י
screens.text:
י is called Yod. It can represent /y/, as at the start of yes. Its small shape is Guy’s “itsy-bitsy” reminder.
יָם — sea
Here י starts the /y/ sound. You also see י in the supplied spellings מַיִם and יַיִן. Read those as complete word models: /ma-yim/ and /ya-yin/. The two י letters in יין belong to this word’s spelling; a fuller spelling comparison comes later.
assets: IMAGE AHY-YOD: original itsy-bitsy mnemonic. AUDIO AHY-YAM, AHY-MAYIM, AHY-YAYIN: sea, water and wine, separately.
IMAGES AHY-SEA, AHY-WATER, AHY-WINE: coastline; water being poured into a glass; clearly labelled wine bottle beside a glass. Wine must not be identifiable merely by liquid colour.

screens.title: A portion on the plate
screens.text:
מָנָה — a portion or dish of food.
מַתָּנָה — a gift.
These words share familiar letters but have different meanings. Listen to the complete word and choose the matching situation. A serving of food is מנה; a present for someone is מתנה.
assets: IMAGE AHY-PORTION: one plated serving of food. AUDIO AHY-MANA: מנה.

interaction.prompt: Which word labels a portion of food?

feedback.מתנה: מתנה is a gift. The portion of food is מנה.
feedback.מנה: Yes. מנה is a portion or dish of food.

screens.title: Read, then reveal
screens.text:
You now have six words. On each vocabulary card, listen, look at the Hebrew, and connect it to the meaning. Then hide the meaning and try to recover it.
You may reveal the vowel marks when you need them. Reading support is there to help you connect the written word to its spoken form.

check.prompt: Which new letter can represent /y/, as in the beginning of ים?

feedback.א: The first letter of ים is י. א has different roles in the supplied words.
feedback.ה: ה can represent /h/. The first letter here is י.
feedback.י: Yes: י starts the /y/ sound in ים.

lessons.title: Introduce yourself: nominal sentences and אני
lessons.anchor: Build an introduction from a speaker, a familiar name and a supplied role word.
lessons.outcome: Say who you are using אני, a name, and one of the supplied role forms.
lessons.sources: Presentation slide 45; Masterfile rows 6, 14, 28 and 595; A2 row 9. New connective text and exercises are proposed wording.
lessons.decisions: Keep the approved three-meaning exception. Teach artist and manager as role nouns; no present-tense paradigm. Artist feminine is supplied from the current plan, with exact pointing subject to review. Minimal sheva support is word-specific.

screens.title: One word for I
screens.text:
אֲנִי — I.
Use אני when you talk about yourself. It stays the same for a man or a woman.
הַיי, אֲנִי מַתָּן.
Hi, I’m Matan.
Matan is an example name. Replace it with your own name when you speak. You can say your own name even if you have not learned how to spell it in Hebrew.
assets: AUDIO NOMINAL-ANI: אני. AUDIO NOMINAL-MATAN: היי, אני מתן. Native recording with a natural pause after the greeting.
Example names: מתן / Matan and תמי / Tami. These are supplied names, not vocabulary targets.

screens.title: A complete introduction
screens.text:
English says “I am Matan.” In this simple Hebrew introduction, אני מתן is already complete. There is no separate word for am.
אֲנִי תָּמִי.
I’m Tami.
Keep the order: the person first, then the identity. We are learning these present-time identity sentences; we are not making a rule about every Hebrew sentence.

interaction.prompt: Which gives the complete introduction “I’m Tami”?

Yes. אני followed by the name makes this introduction.
For this model, put אני before the name.
Use אני once, then the name.

screens.title: Introduce a role
screens.text:
אָמָּן — artist, masculine form.
אָמָּנִית — artist, feminine form.
אֲנִי אָמָּן. — I’m an artist.
אֲנִי אָמָּנִית. — I’m an artist.
Learn these as a supplied pair. Here we are not deriving a general rule for forming feminine words.
assets: AUDIO NOMINAL-ARTIST-M and NOMINAL-ARTIST-F: אמן; אמנית. AUDIO NOMINAL-ARTIST-SENTENCES: אני אמן; אני אמנית.
IMAGE NOMINAL-ARTISTS: two separate character cards explicitly described as an artist using the masculine/feminine form; avoid inferring occupation from appearance.

screens.title: Another role pair
screens.text:
מְנַהֵל — manager, masculine form.
מְנַהֶלֶת — manager, feminine form.
אֲנִי מְנַהֵל.
אֲנִי מְנַהֶלֶת.
Listen to the beginning of these words: the two dots below מ are read with an audible /e/ in these models. Say the complete word with the recording. We will compare that sign with another familiar word in the second vowel lesson.
assets: AUDIO NOMINAL-MANAGER-M and NOMINAL-MANAGER-F: מנהל; מנהלת, with the intended initial /e/. AUDIO NOMINAL-MANAGER-SENTENCES: אני מנהל; אני מנהלת.

screens.title: Put the pieces together
screens.text:
הַיי, אֲנִי תָּמִי. אֲנִי מְנַהֶלֶת.
Hi, I’m Tami. I’m a manager.
This introduction has a greeting, a name and a role. Listen once, then try the introduction with the supplied character details. Your own introduction only needs information that is true for you.

screens.title: Talk to one person
screens.text:
When you speak to one man, use אַתָּה — you. When you speak to one woman, use אַתְּ — you.
אַתָּה מַתָּן. — You are Matan.
אַתְּ תָּמִי. — You are Tami.
The final two-dot sign in אַתְּ adds no extra vowel in this word: listen to /at/. Compare the complete word with the recording.
assets: AUDIO QUESTIONS-ATA and QUESTIONS-AT: אתה; את. AUDIO QUESTIONS-STATEMENTS: אתה מתן; את תמי.
CHARACTERS: identify the addressee explicitly as one man named Matan or one woman named Tami.

screens.title: Ask using the same words
screens.text:
אַתָּה אָמָּן. — You are an artist.
אַתָּה אָמָּן? — Are you an artist?
The word order stays the same in these examples. In speech, the question is carried by the way you say it; in writing, use a question mark. Listen to both versions, then try the question.

feedback.Recording A: A states אתה אמן. Listen again to the question in B.
feedback.Recording B: Yes. B asks אתה אמן? The words and order stay the same.

screens.title: Put who first
screens.text:
מִי — who?
מִי אַתָּה? — Who are you? (to one man)
מִי אַתְּ? — Who are you? (to one woman)
Put מי first in these questions. Answer with an introduction you already know:
מִי אַתְּ? — אֲנִי תָּמִי.
Who are you? — I’m Tami.

screens.title: Address a group
screens.text:
אַתֶּם — you, to an all-male or mixed group.
אַתֶּן — you, to an all-female group.
All four you forms start with את: אתה, את, אתם, אתן. Connect the shared beginning to the shared meaning, then notice who is being addressed.
מִי אַתֶּם?
אֲנִי מַתָּן. אֲנִי תָּמִי.
Who are you? Each person can answer with their own name. No plural role word is needed.

screens.title: Ask for clarification
screens.text:
מָה? — What?
Use this short question when you did not catch what someone said.
אֲנִי תָּמִי. — מָה? — תָּמִי.
I’m Tami. — What? — Tami.
Here מי asks about a person’s identity; מה asks what was said.

מילה means a word. אמת means truth. For these two, use the English explanation on the card rather than trying to guess from a picture.
These are new words to recognise and retrieve. You do not need to force each one into an identity question.

lessons.title: Letters 3: ו: sound roles and third-person pronouns
lessons.anchor: Link a new letter to supplied sounds, then contrast speaking to people with speaking about them.
lessons.outcome: Read the supplied roles of ו, use third-person pronouns, and offer a choice with או.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 65–68; Masterfile third-person rows and lexical rows; current A2 row 11.
lessons.decisions: No consonant-doubling rule here. Consonantal /v/ is demonstrated in a labelled syllable rather than adding an unplanned word. Plural pronouns are used in questions, without untaught plural predicates. The conjunction ו־ waits until lesson 10.

screens.title: One letter, several roles
screens.text:
Meet ו, called Vav. In a supplied consonant-and-vowel model such as וַ, it represents /v/: /va/.
The same letter also appears in vowel spellings:
וֹ — /o/
וּ — /u/
Listen to each model and notice where the dot sits. We will use these forms in words now and compare alternative vowel signs in the next lesson.
assets: AUDIO VAV-VA, VAV-O, VAV-U: /va/, /o/, /u/. וַ is a decoding syllable, not a vocabulary item.
DIAGRAM VAV-DOTS: show וַ, וֹ, וּ separately; highlight the top dot for /o/ and the middle dot for /u/.

screens.title: Offer a choice
screens.text:
אוֹ — or.
תּוּת — strawberry.
תְּאֵנָה אוֹ תּוּת? — תּוּת.
Fig or strawberry? — Strawberry.
You already know תאנה. Put או between the two choices. These are short, useful choices in a real situation; you do not need a full sentence to offer the two fruits.
assets: AUDIO VAV-FRUIT: תאנה או תות? — תות. Model the whole exchange.
IMAGE VAV-FRUIT: a fig and a strawberry, each independently selectable; response has one chosen fruit.

screens.title: Talk about a person
screens.text:
הוּא — he.
הִיא — she.
מִי הוּא? — הוּא מַתָּן.
Who is he? — He is Matan.
מִי הִיא? — הִיא תָּמִי.
Who is she? — She is Tami.
Compare talking to someone with talking about them: אתה addresses a man; הוא refers to him while you talk to someone else.
assets: AUDIO VAV-HE-SHE: הוא; היא; מי הוא? — הוא מתן; מי היא? — היא תמי.
DIAGRAM VAV-REFERENCE: labelled speaker and listener, with Matan/Tami as the third person discussed. Do not infer pronouns merely from an unlabelled picture.

screens.title: Talk about a group
screens.text:
הֵם — they, for an all-male or mixed group.
הֵן — they, for an all-female group.
מִי הֵם? — Who are they?
מִי הֵן? — Who are they?
אתם and אתן speak to the group. הם and הן talk about the group. Keep that difference even when the people are the same.
For now, you can identify the people one at a time: הוא מתן. היא תמי.

lessons.title: Vowels 2: o/u signs, sheva and לא
lessons.anchor: Compare new written signs with known sounds and revisit sheva in two familiar words.
lessons.outcome: Recognise the supplied o/u signs, distinguish the two demonstrated sheva readings and negate an identity with לא.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 75–82; current A2 row 12; earlier vowel draft adapted.
lessons.decisions: This is the approved focused split: no new lexical quota. Source “stop vowel” wording is narrowed; sheva is not universally silent. Kubbutz is taught through a syllable, not an added word.

screens.title: The o sound with and without ו
screens.text:
You have heard /o/ in אוֹ. A dot above the line can also mark /o/ without a ו.
מוֹ — /mo/
מֹ — /mo/
Read the supplied pair and compare it with the recordings. These are syllable examples. Recognising both spellings does not mean replacing one with the other in any word you choose.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS2-O-PAIR: מוֹ; מֹ, both /mo/. Display the dot precisely above the appropriate character.

screens.title: Two written routes to u
screens.text:
You have heard /u/ in תּוּת and הוּא. The וּ spelling is called shuruk. Three diagonal dots below a letter are called kubbutz.
מוּ — /mu/
מֻ — /mu/
Both supplied syllables have /u/. Recognise the three-dot sign; there is no new word to memorise here.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS2-U-PAIR: מוּ; מֻ, both /mu/.

interaction.prompt: Which syllable has the three diagonal dots for /u/?

feedback.מִ: The single dot is /i/ in this example.
feedback.מֶ: These e dots are arranged differently.

screens.title: Return to two familiar words
screens.text:
Compare two words you already know:
אַתְּ — you, to one woman.
מְנַהֵל — manager.
The two vertical dots are called sheva. In the supplied word אַתְּ, they add no vowel after the final consonant. In מְנַהֵל, the model has an audible /e/ at the beginning.
Do not give every sheva the same reading. For now, connect each familiar word to its native spoken model.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS2-SHEVA-AT and VOWELS2-SHEVA-MANAGER: את and מנהל. Play separately; provide an optional replay of the beginning of מנהל, cut from the same native recording after author review.

screens.title: No, and not
screens.text:
לֹא means no. It also means not before the identity you are correcting.
הוּא לֹא מַתָּן. הוּא אָמָּן.
He is not Matan. He is an artist.
Or correct a role:
הִיא לֹא אָמָּנִית. הִיא מְנַהֶלֶת.
She is not an artist. She is a manager.
The word לא comes before the name or role being negated.
assets: AUDIO VOWELS2-LO: לא. AUDIO VOWELS2-CORRECT-M and VOWELS2-CORRECT-F: the two complete correction models.
CONTEXT VOWELS2-CORRECTION: make the asserted identity explicitly false in an English character card. Do not expect learners to infer a stranger’s name or occupation from appearance.

lessons.title: Prepositions and prefixes 1: מ־/ה־/ו־
lessons.anchor: Attach a small meaning to a known word, then reuse the result in an ordinary exchange.
lessons.outcome: Use מ־, ה־ and ו־ in supplied contexts, distinguish day/today and night/tonight, and ask when.
lessons.sources: Presentation slides 42–45 and conjunction material; Masterfile prefix/time notes; current A2 row 13.
lessons.decisions: Exact prefix readings are supplied, not derived from a blanket vowel rule. Time expressions are specific meanings, not a general “ה means this” rule. All seven lexical additions and three prefixes receive practice; integration remains in the following lesson.

screens.title: Point to the known gift
screens.text:
מַתָּנָה means a gift. To say the gift, attach ה to the beginning:
הַמַּתָּנָה — the gift.
A prefix is a small part attached at the beginning of a word. There is no space between ה and מתנה.
Compare a gift being introduced with the particular gift both speakers are now talking about.
assets: AUDIO PREFIX-THE-GIFT: מתנה; המתנה. IMAGE PREFIX-GIFT: first a gift, then the same gift clearly referred to by both speakers.

screens.title: Say where it came from
screens.text:
Attach מ to say from:
מֵאִמָּא — from mother.
מִתָּמִי — from Tami.
הַמַּתָּנָה מֵאִמָּא.
The gift is from mother.
The simple sentence needs no separate word for is. Listen to each complete prefixed form; the vowel after מ is not identical in every context.
assets: AUDIO PREFIX-FROM-MOTHER, PREFIX-FROM-TAMI, PREFIX-GIFT-MOTHER: מאמא; מתמי; המתנה מאמא.
PREFIX animation: attach מ to אמא and תמי without inserting a space. Retain the supplied whole-word readings.

screens.title: Two prefixes in a meaningful context
screens.text:
הַמַּיִם מֵהַיָּם.
The water is from the sea.
You know מים and ים. In מהים, מ adds from and ה marks the sea. Read the whole supplied form with the recording.
הַמַּתָּנָה מֵאִמָּא אוֹ מִתָּמִי? — הַמַּתָּנָה מֵאִמָּא.
Is the gift from mother or from Tami? — The gift is from mother.
assets: AUDIO PREFIX-WATER-SEA and PREFIX-GIFT-CHOICE: the two complete models.
CONTEXT PREFIX-WATER: sample water collected from the sea; the visual makes its origin explicit.

screens.title: Join two familiar items
screens.text:
You know או for or. To join two items with and, attach ו to the second item.
מַיִם וְתֵה. — Water and tea.
מַיִם אוֹ תֵּה? — Water or tea?
The first includes both. The second offers a choice. ו is attached to the following word; או is a separate word. Follow the supplied pronunciation of ותה.
assets: AUDIO PREFIX-AND and PREFIX-OR: מים ותה; מים או תה?

interaction.prompt: Which includes both water and tea?

Yes. ו joins the two items with and.
feedback.מים או תה?: או offers a choice between them.

screens.title: Ask when
screens.text:
יוֹם — day. הַיּוֹם — today.
לַיְלָה — night. הַלַּיְלָה — tonight.
Learn today and tonight as the time expressions used here. Do not assume that ה always means this.
מָתַי? — When?
מָתַי? — הַיּוֹם אוֹ הַלַּיְלָה? — הַלַּיְלָה.
When? — Today or tonight? — Tonight.
You already know how to place a question word first. מתי adds a new meaning to that familiar question pattern.
assets: AUDIO PREFIX-TIMES: יום; היום; לילה; הלילה; מתי. AUDIO PREFIX-WHEN: the three-turn exchange.
CONTEXT PREFIX-MEETING: two people are arranging a meeting, stated in English; no untaught Hebrew word for meeting is required.

screens.title: Two useful words for the situation
screens.text:
הָמוֹן — a lot.
הָמוֹן מַיִם. — A lot of water.
אוּלָם — a hall or auditorium.
Connect המון to a large amount of something familiar. Connect אולם to the pictured indoor hall. We will use these meanings again when more sentence patterns are available.
assets: AUDIO PREFIX-HAMON, PREFIX-ULAM, PREFIX-MUCH-WATER: המון; אולם; המון מים.
IMAGE PREFIX-HALL: an indoor auditorium or large hall; English prompt identifies it as a hall. IMAGE PREFIX-WATER-AMOUNT: clearly large amount of water, not a counted set of bottles.

Yes. ה identifies the gift and מ marks its source.

או means or and does not express the source.

Multiple choice

Display every authored option. Keep the written order for an initial build; if shuffling is later enabled, attach feedback to option identity, not its letter. A selected option alone reveals nothing: Select → Check → feedback. Correct: Continue. Incorrect: Retry or Reveal answer, followed by an opportunity to answer again. Mark attempted-with-help separately from independent correctness; do not invent a numeric mastery threshold.
Typed and ordering

Typed: prompt → attempt → Check → answer-specific feedback; trim surrounding spaces, collapse repeated spaces, ignore case for English-letter reading answers, and allow only the stated alternatives. “I cannot recall yet” reveals a model, then permits a retry. Ordering: show exactly the supplied token pool, use an RTL answer area, Check only after placement, then compare with the specified order. Punctuation is supplied separately unless it is the target.
Matching and self-check

Matching: show all listed prompts and the full response pool, one-to-one unless stated otherwise. Check after all pairs; retain correct pairs and retry misses. Self-check: spoken or written attempt → Reveal model → learner marks Matches / Needs practice. Open personal responses use the stated criteria, never a single exact-string grader. An inaccessible audio/image task must have an equivalent meaningful alternative; if the tested listening skill cannot be provided, label that skill untested rather than pretend text measures it.
Vocabulary display and practice

Cards show meaning, pronunciation, current forms and learner notes. Do not show future plurals, roots, patterns or conjugations merely because they exist in the source. Source fields are preserved verbatim as author reference; absent fields mean not supplied, not necessarily inapplicable. Full/standard/curated display forms are explicit proposed fields; curated initially equals full. Unbound entries have no approved root, paradigm or media inferred for them. All recordings below are required placeholders until verified. The Vocabulary stage has study/reveal controls but no hidden extra graded exercises; all checks are authored explicitly below. Practice may combine several words in a coherent exchange. Separate meaning retrieval is appropriate when sentence grammar is not yet available.
